description_full: Millicom International Cellular S.A. engages in the provision cable and mobile services in Latin America. The company offers mobile services, including mobile data and voice, and short message services; and mobile financial services, such as payments, money transfers, international remittances, savings, real-time loans, and micro-insurance. In addition, the company provides fixed services, including broadband, fixed voice, and pay-TV; and fixed-voice and data telecommunications services, managed services, cloud and security solutions, and value-added services; and tower infrastructure and services. The company serves small, medium, and large businesses, as well as residential consumers and governmental entities. It markets its products and services under the Tigo and Tigo Business brands. The company was founded in 1990 and is headquartered in Luxembourg, Luxembourg.

financial_summary: Millicom International Cellular is a large-cap communication services business with a $13.3B market cap on $5.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 72% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $1.1B in free cash flow — roughly 19 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.27× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.8× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 2.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 8.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 46% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.2) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Payout ratio of 89% leaves thin coverage if earnings wobble
Advertising-cycle exposure and content/regulatory risk — a single platform policy shift or ad-spend contraction cascades through the P&L quickly.
Cord-cutting acceleration and audience fragmentation — legacy distribution bundles unravel faster than subscription revenue can replace them.
AI-generated content commoditisation — as creation costs collapse toward zero, content libraries lose pricing power and differentiation narrows.

sect: Its 28% operating margin runs 20pp above the Communication Services median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.37x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+12.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 171 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 67% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 14% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 26% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 43% and a beta of 0.72, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.34 vs 5y 0.57), so read it loosely.
About $75.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 59% in the 2020 crash and 64% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 63% below its DCF fair value of $212, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 76%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $150 to $310 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Communication Services peers: cheaper on EV/EBITDA 7.0 vs 9.9, richer on P/E 23.5 vs 15.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 45% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 8.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 8 covering analysts target $98.14 on average, 24% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.8%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.54).
It runs a 72% gross margin and converts 19% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.27x.
ROE of 37% is amplified by 4.7x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 11pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.8x net debt to EBITDA ($1.6B of cash against $6.7B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, and interest cover is thin at 2.3x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.24 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.1% over 3 years and 6.9% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 40.4% a year over five years.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 12.3% on average.
Analysts expect 42.1% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 46.0%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 48%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $8.3M sold).
It returns 8.8% a year to shareholders (0.9% in buybacks and 3.8% in dividends).
The share count has grown 10.7% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 19,000 employees, each generates about $306K of revenue, 0.5x the Communication Services median, and revenue has grown 5.2% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $57K of free cash flow per employee.
